content_blocks.title: Why this matters
content_blocks.text: Map, Filter, and Reduce is one step in Apply Functions and Functional Programming; the apply family and purrr tools help express repeated transformations; simplification rules can change result shape. The example is intentionally small so you can predict its result before checking it in a local R session.

content_blocks.title: Work through it
content_blocks.text: Choose the simplest mapper that makes expected result structure obvious and test type stability. Change one input or condition at a time, compare the observed result with your prediction, and write down one limitation.

content_blocks.title: R example: Map, Filter, and Reduce
content_blocks.code:
# Lesson 76: Map, Filter, and Reduce
parts <- list(first = 8:9, second = 10:11)
vapply(parts, sum, numeric(1))

content_blocks.title: Common pitfall
content_blocks.text: Do not treat a syntactically plausible example as proof of correctness. For map, filter, and reduce, check the input type, missing/empty cases, output shape, and domain assumptions.

common_mistakes.problem: Using an example without checking its inputs or output shape.
common_mistakes.why: R can coerce types, propagate missing values or simplify results unexpectedly.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect with str(), class(), typeof(), length() or dim() and add a direct check.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating a demonstration as proof that every edge case works.
common_mistakes.why: Empty input, missing values, dependencies and version differences can change behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Test a normal case and a boundary/failure case in a clean local R session.
